summary: On Resurrection Sunday, Jesus joins two grieving disciples walking to Emmaus, explains from all the Scriptures why the Christ had to suffer, and is recognized as He breaks bread.
key_insight: The two already had the facts: the empty tomb, the angels’ message, and friends who had checked the tomb. What they lacked was the meaning. Their eyes stayed closed to Him until He had shown them from Moses and the Prophets that the Christ had to suffer.
story: That same day, two of Jesus’ followers were walking from Jerusalem to a village called Emmaus, about seven miles away, talking over everything that had happened. As they talked and reasoned, Jesus Himself drew near and went with them. But their eyes were restrained, so that they did not know Him. {Lk} Mark says He appeared “in another form.” {Mk}

He asked them, “What kind of conversation is this that you have with one another as you walk and are sad?” One of them, named Cleopas, answered, “Are You the only stranger in Jerusalem, and have You not known the things which happened there in these days?” “What things?” Jesus asked. {Lk}

They told Him about Jesus of Nazareth, “a Prophet mighty in deed and word before God and all the people,” and how the chief priests and rulers had handed Him over to be condemned and crucified. “But we were hoping that it was He who was going to redeem Israel.” Now it was the third day. Women of their company had gone to the tomb early, found no body, and said angels had told them He was alive. Others had gone and found the tomb just as the women said, “but Him they did not see.” {Lk}

Then Jesus said to them, “O foolish ones, and slow of heart to believe in all that the prophets have spoken! Ought not the Christ to have suffered these things and to enter into His glory?” And beginning at Moses and all the Prophets, He explained to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning Himself. {Lk}
As they came near the village, He made as if to go farther. But they urged Him, “Abide with us, for it is toward evening, and the day is far spent.” So He went in to stay with them. {Lk}

When He sat at the table with them, He took bread, blessed and broke it, and gave it to them. Then their eyes were opened and they knew Him, and He vanished from their sight. They said to one another, “Did not our heart burn within us while He talked with us on the road, and while He opened the Scriptures to us?” {Lk}
The two went back and told the rest, but they did not believe them either. {Mk}
differences: Luke tells the whole story, names Cleopas and gives the distance to Emmaus. Mark tells it in two sentences and does not name the village or the travelers.
Luke says the two did not know Jesus because their eyes “were restrained”; Mark says He appeared “in another form.”
Only Luke records the conversation on the road, the teaching from Moses and the Prophets, and the breaking of bread.
Mark says the others did not believe the two. Luke says that when they arrived, the gathered disciples were saying, “The Lord is risen indeed, and has appeared to Simon!” (Luke 24:34).

fit.question: Mark says the others did not believe the two from Emmaus. Luke says the others greeted them with “The Lord is risen indeed.” Did the disciples believe or not?

points.label: Luke shows the doubt too
points.text: Minutes later, when Jesus stood among them, the same group “supposed they had seen a spirit,” and even after He showed His hands and feet they “still did not believe for joy” (Luke 24:37, 41). Luke himself shows that belief that evening was unsettled.

points.label: Some believed, some did not
points.text: Some in the room were ready to believe because of Peter’s report, while others still doubted, especially a story in which the two had walked for miles without recognizing Him. Mark’s statement does not require that every person doubted, and Luke’s does not require that every person believed.

points.label: Mark’s next verse
points.text: Mark goes on to say that Jesus rebuked the eleven that evening “because they did not believe those who had seen Him after He had risen” (Mark 16:14). Joyful words and lingering unbelief were both in the room.

fit.note: Both writers report the same evening truthfully: a room where joy and doubt were mixed. Their frankness about the disciples’ unbelief is a mark of honest witnesses.
fit.short: Belief that evening was mixed. Luke himself says the group still doubted when Jesus appeared minutes later (Luke 24:37–41).

scene.label: Emmaus
scene.text: Luke puts the village about seven miles from Jerusalem, a walk of two or three hours. Its exact site is uncertain. Several villages have been proposed, and none has been proven.

scene.label: Cleopas
scene.text: Nothing more is known of him for certain. Some think he is the Clopas whose wife Mary stood near the cross (John 19:25), which would make his companion possibly his wife. The names are similar but not identical, so this remains a possibility.

scene.label: “Redeem Israel”
scene.text: Many Jews hoped for a Messiah who would set Israel free from Rome, as God had once redeemed Israel from Egypt. The two had placed that hope in Jesus, and the cross seemed to end it.

scene.label: Moses and the Prophets
scene.text: Luke does not list the passages Jesus explained. In Acts, the apostles preach Christ from Deuteronomy 18:15 (Acts 3:22), Psalm 16 (Acts 2:25–28) and Isaiah 53 (Acts 8:32–35), and these were likely among them.

scene.label: The manuscripts
scene.text: Mark’s brief account comes from Mark 16:9–20. The NKJV includes these verses and notes that some of the oldest manuscripts do not have them.

witnesses.mark: Mark’s longer ending gives the walk only two sentences. His phrase “in another form” is the briefest explanation of why two followers could walk for miles beside Jesus without knowing Him. For Mark, the walk is one more report the others heard and did not accept (16:13).
witnesses.luke: Luke alone tells the full story, one of the richest scenes in his Gospel. He names Cleopas, gives the distance, and shows Jesus opening the Scriptures, a theme he repeats later in the same chapter (24:45). Jesus is made known at a meal, as so often in Luke, and His actions with the bread echo the Last Supper (22:19).

seeing.reveals: The risen Jesus walks beside disappointed followers, lets them pour out their grief, and then shows that His suffering was not the end of their hope but the very road the prophets said the Christ would take into His glory.
seeing.living: Jesus did not first show them His hands. He opened the Scriptures until their hearts burned, and only then let them see Him. When your hopes have collapsed, take your questions to the whole Bible and ask Him to show you Himself there; He may be nearer on that road than you know.
seeing.ponder: What did you hope Jesus would do that He has not done, and could His way through suffering be better than the plan you had for Him?

preaching.big_idea: Jesus turns dead hopes into burning hearts by showing Himself in the Scriptures.
outline: Hearing Christ in all the Scriptures (25–27)
preaching.watch_for: Watch the eyes: at first “their eyes were restrained” (24:16), and at the table “their eyes were opened” (24:31). Between the two, He opens the Scriptures to them (24:27, 32). Luke uses one Greek verb for opened eyes, opened Scriptures and, later, opened understanding (24:31, 32, 45).

title: On the Road to Emmaus
